case: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 9-month history of aching pain in her ribs, hips, and lower legs and increasing difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair. She had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 7 years ago and stopped taking her prescribed supplements 3 years ago. Physical examination shows tenderness to pressure over the ribs and tibiae, weakness of the hip flexors, and a waddling gait. Laboratory studies show: calcium 8.3 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), phosphate 2.1 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), alkaline phosphatase 312 U/L (40 to 120), parathyroid hormone 131 pg/mL (10 to 65), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 7 ng/mL (30 to 100). Serum creatinine and aminotransferase activities are within the reference ranges. Diagnosis: osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency.

questions.stem: Radiographs of the pelvis and femurs are obtained. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Coarse trabeculae with cortical thickening and bone enlargement
Multiple lytic lesions with sharply punched-out margins
Bilateral transverse lucent bands in the femoral necks
Subchondral cysts with osteophytes and joint space narrowing
approach: Link the low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, high PTH, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D to defective mineralization of osteoid in an adult.
Recall that unmineralized osteoid cannot carry normal loads, so it develops incomplete stress fractures that do not heal.
Pick the radiographic sign of these pseudofractures, called Looser zones.
questions.why: Osteomalacia is defective mineralization of new osteoid after the growth plates have closed. Soft, poorly mineralized bone develops Looser zones, also called pseudofractures. These are narrow lucent bands that run across the cortex, often on both sides, at the femoral necks, pubic rami, ribs, and lateral border of the scapula. The rest of the skeleton often looks diffusely osteopenic.
whyNot: This describes Paget disease of bone, which also raises alkaline phosphatase. In Paget disease, calcium, phosphate, and PTH are usually normal, and the bone is enlarged and dense.
Punched-out lytic lesions suggest multiple myeloma. Myeloma causes bone pain, but it tends to raise calcium and does not lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Correct.
These are findings of osteoarthritis, a disease of articular cartilage. They do not explain diffuse bone pain or the mineral abnormalities here.

topics: Laboratory pattern of vitamin D deficiency

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her vitamin D deficiency?
options: Poor absorption of fat-soluble vitamin D from the small bowel
Reduced 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D in the kidney
Reduced 25-hydroxylation of cholecalciferol in the liver
Increased hepatic catabolism of vitamin D by induced cytochrome P450
approach: Note that 25-hydroxyvitamin D is very low, so the problem is in the supply of vitamin D that reaches the liver.
Normal creatinine and aminotransferases argue against kidney or liver disease, and no enzyme-inducing drug is listed.
Roux-en-Y bypass sends food past the duodenum and proximal jejunum and delays mixing with bile, so fat-soluble vitamins are poorly absorbed.
questions.why: Vitamin D is fat soluble. It is absorbed with dietary fat in bile salt micelles in the small intestine. After Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, food skips the duodenum and proximal jejunum and meets bile only further down in the common channel, so less vitamin D is absorbed. Without supplements, her stores ran down over years. A low 25-hydroxyvitamin D level shows that the body is short of substrate.
whyNot: Correct.
Kidney failure lowers calcitriol, but 25-hydroxyvitamin D stays normal. Her creatinine is normal and her 25-hydroxyvitamin D is very low.
Severe liver disease can impair 25-hydroxylation, but her aminotransferases are normal, and the liver has a large reserve for this step.
Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants such as phenytoin speed vitamin D breakdown. She takes no such drug.

topics: Risk factors for vitamin D deficiency
Fat-soluble vitamin absorption after bariatric surgery

questions.stem: She is started on oral cholecalciferol. Her physician plans to follow serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D rather than 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D to judge when her stores are restored. Which of the following best explains this choice?
options: It binds the vitamin D receptor with the highest affinity
It is formed directly in the skin by ultraviolet B light
Its production in the kidney is stimulated by PTH
It is long-lived and its synthesis tracks supply
approach: Trace the pathway: 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin to cholecalciferol, then hepatic 25-hydroxylation, then renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation.
Ask which step is tightly controlled by hormones and which simply follows the amount of substrate.
The best marker of stores is the long-lived form whose level follows supply.
questions.why: UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin to cholecalciferol, which also comes from the diet. The liver adds a 25-hydroxyl group with little feedback control, so 25-hydroxyvitamin D rises and falls with supply and circulates for about 2 to 3 weeks. The kidney then makes calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) under tight control by PTH, phosphate, and FGF23. Calcitriol lasts only hours, and in deficiency the high PTH can keep it normal or even high, so it is a poor measure of stores.
whyNot: Calcitriol is the form that binds the vitamin D receptor most strongly and acts as the hormone.
The skin makes cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) from 7-dehydrocholesterol. The 25-hydroxylation step happens in the liver.
PTH stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which makes calcitriol. 25-hydroxyvitamin D is made in the liver.
Correct.

topics: Why 25-hydroxyvitamin D measures vitamin D status

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms most directly accounts for her low serum phosphate concentration?
options: FGF23 excess reducing renal phosphate reabsorption
PTH excess reducing renal phosphate reabsorption
Insulin-driven shift of phosphate into cells
Rapid uptake of phosphate into remineralizing bone
approach: Vitamin D deficiency lowers intestinal calcium absorption, and the falling calcium stimulates the parathyroid glands.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism follows, and PTH is high in this case.
PTH removes sodium-phosphate cotransporters from the proximal tubule, so phosphate is lost in the urine.
questions.why: In vitamin D deficiency the gut absorbs less calcium, and PTH rises to defend serum calcium. PTH increases bone resorption by raising RANKL on osteoblasts, increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, and stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase. It also lowers phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule. The result is a calcium that is low or low-normal and a clearly low phosphate. Reduced gut absorption of phosphate adds to this, but PTH-driven urinary loss is the main cause.
whyNot: FGF23 excess causes phosphate wasting in X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets and tumor-induced osteomalacia. In those disorders PTH and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are usually normal.
Correct.
Insulin moves phosphate into cells during refeeding. Nothing in her history suggests refeeding.
Hungry bone after parathyroidectomy or early in vitamin D treatment pulls phosphate into bone. Her labs were drawn before any treatment.

dx: Nutritional rickets in an exclusively breastfed toddler
case: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the physician because he is not yet walking steadily and his legs have become bowed. He has been exclusively breastfed and has received no vitamin supplements. He has darkly pigmented skin and lives in a northern city with long winters. Physical examination shows frontal bossing, beading of the costochondral junctions, widened wrists, and bowed legs. Laboratory studies show: calcium 8.1 mg/dL (8.8 to 10.8), phosphate 3.1 mg/dL (3.8 to 6.5), alkaline phosphatase 960 U/L (about 150 to 420), parathyroid hormone 148 pg/mL (10 to 65), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 6 ng/mL (30 to 100). Diagnosis: nutritional rickets due to vitamin D deficiency.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl seen in the same clinic also has bowed legs and widened wrists. Her mother and maternal grandmother are short and have bowed legs. Which of the following sets of laboratory findings would most strongly suggest X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets in the girl?
options: Calcium low, phosphate low, 25-hydroxyvitamin D low, PTH high
Calcium normal, phosphate low, 25-hydroxyvitamin D normal, PTH normal
Calcium high, phosphate high, 25-hydroxyvitamin D high, PTH suppressed
Calcium low, phosphate high, 25-hydroxyvitamin D normal, PTH very high
approach: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets comes from loss of PHEX function, which raises FGF23 from osteocytes.
FGF23 causes renal phosphate wasting and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so phosphate is low while vitamin D stores are normal.
Calcium stays near normal, so PTH is not strongly stimulated. Pick the pattern with an isolated low phosphate.
questions.why: In X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, loss of PHEX function raises FGF23. FGF23 removes sodium-phosphate cotransporters from the proximal tubule and suppresses renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so phosphate is low and calcitriol is low or inappropriately normal. Calcium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and PTH are usually normal or near normal. The skeletal signs look like nutritional rickets, but the disease does not respond to ordinary vitamin D doses. Affected mothers pass it to half their children, which fits this family.
whyNot: This is the pattern of nutritional vitamin D deficiency, as in the boy in this case.
Correct.
High calcium, suppressed PTH, and high 25-hydroxyvitamin D point to vitamin D toxicity, which does not cause rickets.
Low calcium with high phosphate and very high PTH is the pattern of chronic kidney disease, which causes renal osteodystrophy.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the long bones of his legs have bowed?
options: Reduced synthesis of type I collagen by osteoblasts
Reduced bone mass with a normally mineralized matrix
Reduced chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate
Failure of newly formed osteoid to mineralize
approach: Low calcium and low phosphate leave too little mineral for hydroxyapatite crystals to form.
Osteoblasts keep making osteoid, but it stays soft and unmineralized.
Soft bone bends under the weight of a child who is starting to walk.
questions.why: Vitamin D deficiency lowers intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, and secondary hyperparathyroidism adds renal phosphate loss. With too little mineral, the osteoid that osteoblasts lay down cannot form hydroxyapatite. Unmineralized osteoid is flexible, so weight-bearing bones bow. The same defect is called rickets when it occurs before the growth plates close and osteomalacia after they close.
whyNot: Reduced or abnormal type I collagen causes osteogenesis imperfecta, with brittle bones that fracture. The collagen matrix is made normally in rickets.
This describes osteoporosis. The bone that remains is normally mineralized, and calcium, phosphate, and PTH are normal.
Reduced chondrocyte proliferation from FGFR3 gain of function causes achondroplasia, with short limbs and normal mineral levels.
Correct.

topics: Mineralization defect in rickets and osteomalacia

questions.stem: A radiograph of his wrist shows widened, cupped, and frayed distal radial and ulnar metaphyses. A biopsy of the growth plate would most likely show which of the following?
options: A thick, disorganized zone of hypertrophic chondrocytes
A thin, disorganized zone of proliferating chondrocytes
Early fusion of the plate with bony bridging
Dense calcified cartilage cores persisting in the diaphysis
approach: Recall the zones from the epiphysis toward the shaft: reserve, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcification, and ossification.
Hypertrophic chondrocytes need enough phosphate to undergo apoptosis and let their matrix calcify.
Without mineralization the hypertrophic cells pile up, so the plate becomes thick and irregular, seen as a widened, cupped metaphysis.
questions.why: In a normal growth plate, chondrocytes divide in the proliferative zone, enlarge in the hypertrophic zone, and then die as the matrix around them calcifies and is replaced by bone. Low phosphate blocks apoptosis of hypertrophic chondrocytes and mineralization of their matrix. The hypertrophic zone expands and becomes disorganized, and the metaphysis widens and cups on radiographs.
whyNot: Correct.
A thin proliferative zone is the defect in achondroplasia, where FGFR3 gain of function slows chondrocyte proliferation.
Premature closure follows growth plate fractures or early exposure to sex steroids. Rickets widens the plate.
Persistent calcified cartilage cores in dense bone are seen in osteopetrosis, where osteoclasts fail to resorb.

topics: Growth plate in rickets compared with achondroplasia

questions.stem: Two days after a febrile illness, he has spasms of the hands and feet, and tapping over the facial nerve makes the corner of his mouth twitch. Which of the following best explains his increased neuromuscular excitability?
options: Increased acetylcholine release from motor nerve terminals
Increased calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Lower threshold for opening of neuronal sodium channels
Reduced acetylcholinesterase activity at the end plate
approach: Link carpopedal spasm and a Chvostek sign to hypocalcemia.
Extracellular calcium normally binds the outer membrane surface near sodium channels and raises the voltage needed to open them.
When calcium falls, sodium channels open closer to the resting potential, so nerves fire on their own.
questions.why: Extracellular calcium stabilizes excitable membranes. Calcium ions bind negative charges on the outside of the membrane near sodium channel gates, which makes the channels harder to open. In hypocalcemia, a smaller depolarization opens sodium channels, so peripheral nerves fire repeatedly and cause tetany. The Chvostek sign (facial twitch when the facial nerve is tapped) and the Trousseau sign (carpal spasm with a blood pressure cuff) show this excitability.
whyNot: Calcium entry into the nerve terminal triggers acetylcholine release, so low extracellular calcium reduces release.
In skeletal muscle, sarcoplasmic reticulum release is triggered by the T-tubule voltage sensor and does not depend on extracellular calcium.
Correct.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition, as with organophosphates, causes fasciculations and weakness. Hypocalcemia does not affect the enzyme.

dx: Scurvy in an older man with alcohol use disorder
case: A 67-year-old man is brought to the physician by his daughter because of 2 months of fatigue, bleeding gums, easy bruising, and a painful, swollen right knee. He has alcohol use disorder, lives alone, and for the past year has eaten mostly toast, tea, and canned meat with no fruit or vegetables. A shin laceration from 6 weeks ago has not healed. Physical examination shows swollen, purple, friable gums, large ecchymoses on the thighs, and a tense right knee effusion. Laboratory studies show: hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), platelet count 238,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), prothrombin time 12.5 seconds (11 to 13.5), and partial thromboplastin time 31 seconds (25 to 35). Plasma ascorbic acid is 0.1 mg/dL (0.4 to 2.0). Diagnosis: scurvy.

questions.stem: Examination of his skin is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Palpable purpura with IgA deposits in vessel walls
Spider angiomas with radiating small vessels
Rough follicular papules without bleeding
Perifollicular hemorrhages with coiled hairs
approach: Bleeding with a normal platelet count, PT, and PTT points to weak vessel walls, not a clotting factor or platelet problem.
A diet without fruit or vegetables and a very low ascorbic acid level identify vitamin C deficiency.
Weak collagen around hair follicles leads to small bleeds there, and abnormal keratinization produces coiled, corkscrew hairs.
questions.why: Scurvy weakens the collagen that supports small blood vessels. Early skin signs are follicular hyperkeratosis with perifollicular hemorrhages, often on the legs, and coiled corkscrew hairs. Larger bleeds cause ecchymoses, swollen bleeding gums, and hemarthrosis. Coagulation tests are normal because platelets and the clotting cascade are intact. Risk is highest in people who eat no fruit or vegetables, including many with alcohol use disorder.
whyNot: Palpable purpura with IgA deposits is IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura), seen mostly in children after an upper respiratory infection.
Spider angiomas come from high estrogen in chronic liver disease. They are common with heavy alcohol use but do not explain bleeding with normal coagulation tests.
Follicular papules without bleeding fit vitamin A deficiency. Bleeding around the follicle is what points to vitamin C.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following steps in collagen synthesis is most directly impaired in this patient?
options: Cross-linking of lysine residues by lysyl oxidase
Hydroxylation of proline residues in procollagen
Cleavage of terminal propeptides from procollagen
Glycosylation of hydroxylysine residues in procollagen
approach: Vitamin C is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Hydroxyproline forms hydrogen bonds that hold the three alpha chains together in a stable triple helix.
Without it the triple helix is unstable at body temperature and is degraded, so vessel walls and wounds are weak.
questions.why: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need iron in the ferrous state, and ascorbate keeps the iron reduced. Without vitamin C, proline and lysine residues in procollagen are poorly hydroxylated. Underhydroxylated chains form unstable triple helices that are degraded inside the cell, so less collagen is secreted. Capillary walls and healing wounds depend on new collagen, so they bleed and fail to heal.
whyNot: Lysyl oxidase acts outside the cell and needs copper. Its failure is seen in Menkes disease.
Correct.
Procollagen peptidases remove propeptides outside the cell. Defects cause the dermatosparaxis type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Glycosylation does not use vitamin C. It falls only as a downstream effect, because fewer hydroxylysine residues are available.

questions.stem: Aspiration of his right knee yields grossly bloody fluid. Which of the following structures of this synovial joint is the most likely source of the bleeding?
options: Articular hyaline cartilage of the femoral condyles
Inner portion of the medial meniscus
Synovial membrane lining the joint capsule
Calcified cartilage deep to the tidemark
approach: Bleeding needs a vascular tissue that faces the joint cavity.
Articular hyaline cartilage and the inner menisci have no blood vessels and are nourished by synovial fluid.
The synovial membrane has a rich capillary network under its lining cells, so fragile capillaries there bleed into the joint.
questions.why: A synovial joint has articular hyaline cartilage on the bone ends, a cavity filled with synovial fluid, and a capsule lined by synovial membrane. The synovial membrane is a thin layer of synoviocytes that make hyaluronan and lubricin, lying on a loose, highly vascular subintima. In scurvy the walls of these capillaries are weak, so they bleed into the cavity and cause hemarthrosis. Articular cartilage has no vessels at all.
whyNot: Articular hyaline cartilage is avascular and gets its nutrients by diffusion from synovial fluid, so it cannot bleed.
Only the outer third of each meniscus has a blood supply. The inner portion is avascular.
Correct.
The calcified cartilage under the tidemark is avascular and is covered by the articular cartilage, so it does not face the cavity.

questions.stem: Additional studies show a serum calcium of 7.4 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5) with a normal albumin, magnesium 0.8 mg/dL (1.7 to 2.2), and parathyroid hormone 12 pg/mL (10 to 65). His calcium stays low despite intravenous calcium until magnesium is replaced. Which of the following best explains his hypocalcemia?
options: Impaired PTH secretion and action from magnesium depletion
Reduced lysyl oxidase activity from copper depletion
Reduced osteocalcin carboxylation from vitamin K depletion
Reduced renal calcium reabsorption from vitamin C depletion
approach: Low calcium should drive PTH up, yet his PTH is low-normal, so the parathyroid response is blunted.
Severe hypomagnesemia, common in alcohol use disorder, impairs PTH release and makes bone and kidney resistant to PTH.
Calcium corrects only after magnesium is replaced, which confirms the link.
questions.why: Magnesium is needed for the parathyroid glands to secrete PTH and for target tissues to respond to it. In severe magnesium depletion, PTH stays inappropriately low and calcium falls. Alcohol use disorder causes magnesium loss through poor intake, diarrhea, and renal wasting. Calcium given alone does not correct the problem until magnesium is restored. Mild hypomagnesemia can stimulate PTH, and the block appears with severe depletion.
whyNot: Correct.
Copper is the cofactor for lysyl oxidase, which cross-links collagen. Copper deficiency weakens connective tissue but does not lower calcium.
Vitamin K carboxylates osteocalcin and clotting factors. Deficiency affects bone quality and clotting, and his PT is normal.
Vitamin C has no direct role in renal calcium handling.

topics: Mineral and cofactor roles in bone

case: A 26-year-old man comes to the physician because of 2 years of low back and buttock pain with morning stiffness that lasts about 90 minutes. The pain wakes him in the second half of the night, improves with exercise, and does not improve with rest. He has also had heel pain. Physical examination shows tenderness over both sacroiliac joints and at the Achilles tendon insertions. Forward flexion of the lumbar spine is reduced, and chest expansion is 2.0 cm (normal 5 cm or more). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 38 mm/h (0 to 15), and rheumatoid factor is negative. Radiographs show bilateral sacroiliitis with erosions and sclerosis. HLA-B27 testing is positive. Diagnosis: ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the normal function of the HLA molecule linked to his disease?
options: Presents cytosolic peptides to CD8 T cells
Presents endocytosed peptides to CD4 T cells
Presents lipid antigens to NKT cells
Binds immune complexes as a complement protein
approach: HLA-B is one of the three classical MHC class I loci (A, B, and C).
Class I molecules are found on nearly all nucleated cells and display peptides made inside the cell.
Peptides on class I molecules are recognized by CD8 cytotoxic T cells.
questions.why: HLA-B27 is an MHC class I molecule. Like other class I molecules, it carries peptides from cytosolic proteins, cut by the proteasome and loaded in the endoplasmic reticulum, to the cell surface for CD8 T cells. How it causes spondyloarthritis is not fully known. Leading ideas are presentation of cross-reactive microbial peptides, misfolding of HLA-B27 heavy chains that triggers cell stress, and IL-23 and IL-17 driven inflammation at entheses. The result is enthesitis and sacroiliitis that heal with new bone.
whyNot: Correct.
This is the function of MHC class II molecules (HLA-DR, DP, and DQ). HLA-DR4 is linked to rheumatoid arthritis.
CD1d, a nonclassical molecule, presents lipids to NKT cells. HLA-B27 presents peptides.
Complement proteins C2, C4, and factor B are encoded in the MHC class III region. HLA-B27 is not a complement protein.

questions.stem: Twelve years later, a high-pitched, blowing, early diastolic decrescendo murmur is heard along the sternal border while he leans forward. Which of the following hemodynamic findings is most likely?
options: Narrow pulse pressure with a delayed carotid upstroke
Pulsus paradoxus with equal diastolic chamber pressures
Wide pulse pressure with a low diastolic pressure
Large v waves in the jugular venous pulse
approach: An early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the sternal border is aortic regurgitation.
Aortitis in ankylosing spondylitis dilates the aortic root and pulls the cusps apart.
Blood flows back into the ventricle during diastole, so diastolic pressure falls, and the larger stroke volume raises systolic pressure.
questions.why: Ankylosing spondylitis can inflame the aortic root and the base of the valve. The root dilates and the cusps fail to close, causing aortic regurgitation. Backflow during diastole drops aortic diastolic pressure, while the left ventricle ejects a larger stroke volume, raising systolic pressure. The result is a wide pulse pressure with bounding pulses. Other extra-articular features of the disease include anterior uveitis, restrictive lung disease, and fractures of the fused spine.
whyNot: A narrow pulse pressure with a slow, delayed upstroke is aortic stenosis, which causes a systolic ejection murmur.
Pulsus paradoxus with equal diastolic pressures in all chambers is cardiac tamponade.
Correct.
Large v waves suggest tricuspid regurgitation, which causes a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.

questions.stem: As the disease advances, his spine fuses in the forward-flexed posture that eases his pain. Which of the following changes in spinal curvature is most likely?
options: Increased lumbar lordosis and reduced thoracic kyphosis
Loss of lumbar lordosis and increased thoracic kyphosis
Lateral thoracic curvature with vertebral rotation
Increased cervical lordosis with normal thoracic curvature
approach: Recall the normal curves: cervical and lumbar lordosis, and thoracic and sacral kyphosis.
Bony bridges called syndesmophytes join the vertebrae in whatever posture the patient holds.
A forward-flexed posture flattens the lumbar spine and bends the thoracic spine further forward.
questions.why: The adult spine has two curves that are convex forward (cervical and lumbar lordosis) and two that are convex backward (thoracic and sacral kyphosis). In ankylosing spondylitis, inflammation at the vertebral corners and the annulus fibrosus heals with syndesmophytes that fuse the spine, the bamboo spine on radiographs. Patients lean forward for comfort, so the lumbar lordosis is lost and thoracic kyphosis increases. Severe thoracic deformity, like severe scoliosis, stiffens the chest wall and limits lung expansion.
whyNot: Excess lumbar lordosis occurs with pregnancy, obesity, or weak abdominal muscles. Inflammation and fusion in this disease flatten the lumbar spine.
Correct.
Lateral curvature with vertebral rotation is scoliosis, which is usually idiopathic and starts in adolescence.
The cervical spine also stiffens and the head is pushed forward, so cervical lordosis is lost.

questions.stem: His reduced chest expansion is partly due to inflammation and fusion of the posterior synovial joints that let the ribs rise during inspiration. These joints are formed with which of the following vertebral features?
options: Transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae
Bifid spinous processes of the cervical vertebrae
Mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae
Costal facets of the thoracic vertebrae
approach: The ribs move at joints with the vertebrae during breathing, which lifts and widens the chest.
Only thoracic vertebrae carry costal facets on their bodies and transverse processes for the rib heads and tubercles.
Fusion of these synovial joints locks the ribs and limits chest expansion.
questions.why: Each typical rib meets the thoracic spine at two synovial joints. The rib head joins costal facets on the vertebral bodies (costovertebral joint), and the rib tubercle joins the facet on the transverse process (costotransverse joint). Rib elevation at these joints expands the chest during inspiration. Ankylosing spondylitis inflames and fuses these joints, so chest expansion falls and breathing depends more on the diaphragm.
whyNot: Transverse foramina carry the vertebral arteries in the cervical spine. Ribs do not attach there.
Bifid cervical spines anchor the ligamentum nuchae and neck muscles, not ribs.
Mammillary processes on lumbar vertebrae anchor deep back muscles. Lumbar vertebrae have no rib joints.
Correct.

dx: Septic prepatellar bursitis from Staphylococcus aureus
case: A 41-year-old woman who installs floor tile comes to the emergency department because of 3 days of painful swelling over the front of her right knee. She works kneeling most of the day and had several small abrasions on that knee last week. Temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse 98/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a warm, red, fluctuant swelling directly over the patella. She can flex the knee to 120 degrees with pain only at full flexion, and there is no joint effusion. Aspiration of the swelling yields cloudy fluid with 52,000 leukocytes/mm3, 90% neutrophils. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters, and culture grows a catalase-positive, coagulase-positive organism. Diagnosis: septic prepatellar bursitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely route by which the organism reached the bursa?
options: Hematogenous seeding during transient bacteremia
Spread from the adjacent knee joint cavity
Direct entry through overlying skin abrasions
Contiguous spread from osteomyelitis of the patella
approach: The prepatellar bursa lies between the skin and the patella, just under the skin surface.
It does not communicate with the knee joint, which is why knee motion is preserved and there is no effusion.
Superficial bursae such as the prepatellar and olecranon bursae are usually infected by organisms entering through skin breaks over them.
questions.why: Septic bursitis most often involves the superficial prepatellar and olecranon bursae, which take repeated pressure and minor skin injury. Kneeling work causes chronic friction, the cause of most prepatellar bursitis, and abrasions let skin flora such as Staphylococcus aureus enter the bursa directly. Septic arthritis, by contrast, usually follows bacteremia. Deeper bursae, such as the subacromial and trochanteric bursae, are more often inflamed by overuse than infected. Preserved knee motion without an effusion helps tell bursitis from septic arthritis.
whyNot: Hematogenous seeding is the usual route for septic arthritis and for childhood osteomyelitis. It is uncommon for superficial bursae.
The prepatellar bursa does not communicate with the knee joint, and her knee has no effusion.
Correct.
Patellar osteomyelitis is rare and nothing here suggests it. Her skin abrasions over the bursa explain the infection.

questions.stem: The bursal fluid contains IgG antibodies against the organism, yet neutrophils ingest the bacteria poorly. Which of the following bacterial products best explains this finding?
options: M protein
IgA protease
Exfoliative toxin
Protein A
approach: Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase and coagulase positive identify Staphylococcus aureus.
IgG opsonizes bacteria when its Fc region binds Fc receptors on neutrophils.
Staphylococcal protein A binds the Fc region of IgG, so the antibody is held the wrong way round and cannot opsonize.
questions.why: Protein A is a cell wall protein of Staphylococcus aureus that binds the Fc portion of IgG. Antibody bound by its Fc end cannot link the bacterium to neutrophil Fc receptors, and complement activation is reduced, so phagocytosis fails. Other factors help S. aureus cause bone and joint infection: adhesins that bind collagen and fibronectin, and biofilm on prosthetic hardware. Together they make it the most common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.
whyNot: M protein is the main antiphagocytic protein of Streptococcus pyogenes, a catalase-negative organism that grows in chains.
IgA protease is made by Neisseria, Haemophilus influenzae, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. It cleaves IgA at mucosal surfaces and does not act on IgG.
Exfoliative toxin from S. aureus splits desmoglein 1 and causes scalded skin syndrome. It does not block opsonization.
Correct.

questions.stem: If the infection had spread into her knee joint, the articular cartilage could have been destroyed within days. Which of the following most directly causes this rapid cartilage loss?
options: Proteases and oxidants released by neutrophils
Immune complexes activating complement in synovium
Pannus with RANKL-activated osteoclasts
CD8 T cells lysing chondrocytes
approach: Septic arthritis fills the joint with neutrophils, much like the 52,000 cells/mm3 in her bursal fluid.
Activated neutrophils release elastase, collagenases, and reactive oxygen species.
These degrade cartilage matrix within days, much faster than any chronic autoimmune process.
questions.why: In septic arthritis, bacteria in the joint cavity recruit large numbers of neutrophils. Neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinases, and reactive oxygen species break down aggrecan and type II collagen. Cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF also stimulate chondrocytes to release their own proteases. Because cartilage has no blood supply and repairs poorly, damage can be permanent within days, which is why an infected joint is drained urgently.
whyNot: Correct.
Immune complex deposition with complement activation is type III hypersensitivity, as in SLE arthritis, which is usually nonerosive.
Pannus with RANKL-driven osteoclasts erodes cartilage and bone in rheumatoid arthritis over months to years.
CD8 T cells kill cells that show foreign peptides on class I molecules, as in viral infection. They are not the main effectors in acute bacterial joint infection.

questions.stem: After drainage and antibiotics, the skin incision over the bursa heals. Which of the following best describes the main collagen in the granulation tissue at 1 week and in the mature scar months later?
options: Type I at 1 week, replaced by type III in the scar
Type III at 1 week, replaced by type I in the scar
Type II at 1 week, replaced by type I in the scar
Type IV at 1 week, replaced by type III in the scar
approach: Granulation tissue forms first, with new capillaries and fibroblasts laying down a thin, flexible collagen.
That early collagen is type III, the type in reticular fibers and vessel walls.
During remodeling, fibroblasts replace it with stronger type I collagen, the type in tendon, ligament, and bone.
questions.why: Early granulation tissue is rich in type III collagen, which forms thin fibers suited to a new, vascular scaffold. Over weeks to months, matrix metalloproteinases remove it and fibroblasts lay down type I collagen, which has high tensile strength. A mature scar reaches only about 70 to 80 percent of the strength of normal skin. Type II collagen belongs to hyaline cartilage and the nucleus pulposus, and type IV to basement membranes.
whyNot: This reverses the real sequence. Type I collagen is the strong, late collagen of a mature scar.
Correct.
Type II collagen is found in hyaline cartilage, the vitreous, and the nucleus pulposus, not in healing skin.
Type IV collagen forms basement membranes. It does not make up the bulk of granulation tissue or scar.

case: A 43-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 10 months of pain in her neck, shoulders, back, hips, and legs on both sides of the body. She also reports fatigue, waking unrefreshed despite 8 hours in bed, and trouble concentrating at work. Physical examination shows tenderness to light pressure at many soft tissue sites. The joints show no swelling, muscle strength is 5/5 throughout, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric. Laboratory studies show: erythrocyte sedimentation rate 8 mm/h (0 to 20), C-reactive protein 0.3 mg/dL (0 to 0.8), creatine kinase 88 U/L (30 to 170), thyroid-stimulating hormone 1.9 μU/mL (0.5 to 4.5), and a normal complete blood count. Diagnosis: fibromyalgia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her widespread pain?
options: Inflammation of bursae around the shoulders and hips
Increased central amplification of sensory input
CD8 T cell infiltration of skeletal muscle fibers
Denervation of muscle fibers by motor neuron loss
approach: Widespread pain for more than 3 months with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, and poor concentration fits fibromyalgia.
Normal ESR, CRP, CK, strength, and joints rule out inflammation and muscle injury.
The pain comes from increased sensitivity of central pain pathways, so ordinary pressure is felt as pain.
questions.why: Fibromyalgia is a disorder of central pain sensitization. Pathways in the spinal cord and brain amplify incoming signals, and descending pain inhibition is weaker, so pressure that should feel normal is painful. There is no tissue inflammation or muscle damage, which is why inflammatory markers, CK, and the joint examination are normal. It is more common in women and is linked with poor sleep, fatigue, and mood disorders.
whyNot: Bursitis around the shoulder and hip girdles is typical of polymyalgia rheumatica, which occurs after age 50 with a high ESR.
Correct.
CD8 T cell invasion of muscle fibers is polymyositis, which causes proximal weakness and a high CK.
Motor neuron loss causes weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, and reflex changes. Her strength and reflexes are normal.

questions.stem: During the neurologic examination, tapping her patellar tendon produces brisk extension of the knee. Which of the following receptors and spinal cord segments mediate this reflex?
options: Muscle spindle with group Ia afferents, mainly L4
Golgi tendon organ with group Ib afferents, mainly L4
Muscle spindle with group Ia afferents, mainly S1
Golgi tendon organ with group Ib afferents, mainly S1
approach: Tapping the tendon briefly stretches the quadriceps.
Stretch is sensed by muscle spindles, whose group Ia afferents synapse directly on alpha motor neurons to the same muscle.
The patellar reflex runs through L2 to L4, mainly L4. The Achilles reflex tests S1.
questions.why: The patellar reflex is a monosynaptic stretch reflex. A tendon tap stretches the quadriceps and its intrafusal fibers, Ia afferents fire, and they excite alpha motor neurons in the L2 to L4 segments, mainly L4, so the quadriceps contracts. Gamma motor neurons set spindle sensitivity. Golgi tendon organs sit at the muscle-tendon junction, sense tension through Ib afferents, and inhibit the same muscle. Normal reflexes in fibromyalgia fit the absence of nerve or muscle disease.
whyNot: Correct.
Golgi tendon organs sense tension and inhibit the same muscle through Ib afferents. They do not drive the knee jerk.
Muscle spindles and Ia fibers are right, but S1 is the level of the Achilles reflex.
Both parts are wrong. Ib afferents from tendon organs mediate inhibition, and S1 serves the Achilles reflex.

topics: Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs

questions.stem: She begins a graded aerobic walking and cycling program. After 3 months, which of the following changes in her leg muscles is most likely?
options: Hypertrophy of type II fibers with more myofibrils
Conversion of type I fibers into type IIx fibers
Higher glycolytic enzyme activity in type II fibers
Greater mitochondrial and capillary density
approach: Endurance exercise is sustained, low-force work that depends on oxidative metabolism.
Type I fibers are slow, oxidative, and fatigue resistant, and trained muscle adapts by increasing oxidative capacity.
Resistance training, not aerobic training, causes type II fiber hypertrophy.
questions.why: Repeated aerobic exercise increases mitochondrial number and size, oxidative enzymes, myoglobin, and capillary density in trained muscle, mainly in type I and type IIa fibers. These changes let the muscle burn more fatty acid and produce less lactate at a given workload. Heavy resistance training instead enlarges type II fibers by adding myofibrils. Type I fibers look red because of their myoglobin and dense capillary supply.
whyNot: Type II fiber hypertrophy is the main response to heavy resistance training.
Endurance training shifts fibers toward more oxidative types, such as type IIx toward type IIa. It does not convert type I fibers into type IIx.
Endurance training raises oxidative capacity. Sprint and resistance training are the stimuli for higher glycolytic capacity.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her antinuclear antibody test is positive at a titer of 1:80, and she is worried that she has systemic lupus erythematosus. Which of the following antibody results would be most specific for that diagnosis?
options: Anti-CCP
Anti-Scl-70
Anti-Smith
Anti-Jo-1
approach: A low-titer ANA is common in healthy people, especially women, and is not specific.
Disease-specific antibodies are used to confirm a suspected connective tissue disease.
Anti-Smith and anti-dsDNA are highly specific for SLE. The other choices point to other diseases.
questions.why: ANA is sensitive for SLE but not specific, and a titer of 1:80 is found in more than 1 in 10 healthy people. Anti-Smith antibodies, against small nuclear ribonucleoproteins, are highly specific for SLE, though only a minority of patients have them. Anti-dsDNA is also specific and tracks disease activity and lupus nephritis. Her normal inflammatory markers and examination already make SLE unlikely.
whyNot: Anti-CCP is the most specific antibody for rheumatoid arthritis.
Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) marks diffuse systemic sclerosis, with skin thickening and interstitial lung disease.
Correct.
Anti-Jo-1 marks inflammatory myositis with interstitial lung disease.

dx: Acute gout of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
case: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of sudden, severe pain in his right great toe that woke him at 3 AM. The evening before, he drank several beers and ate a large steak dinner. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse 92/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 148/88 mm Hg. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, hot, swollen, and too tender to touch. Serum urate is 9.2 mg/dL (3.5 to 7.2). Aspiration of the joint yields cloudy fluid with 28,000 leukocytes/mm3, mostly neutrophils. Gram stain and culture are negative. Diagnosis: acute gout of the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

questions.stem: Polarized light microscopy of the joint fluid is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence
Needle-shaped crystals with strong positive birefringence
Flat rectangular plates with notched corners
Needle-shaped crystals with strong negative birefringence
approach: Sudden, severe first MTP pain after alcohol and a large meat meal, with high urate and a thiazide, points to gout.
Monosodium urate forms long, thin needles.
Urate crystals are strongly negatively birefringent: yellow when parallel to the compensator axis and blue when perpendicular.
questions.why: Gout is confirmed by finding monosodium urate crystals in joint fluid, often inside neutrophils. They are needle shaped and strongly negatively birefringent, so they look yellow when their long axis lies parallel to the compensator and blue when perpendicular. Other features of gout include tophi (urate deposits in soft tissue), punched-out bone erosions with overhanging edges, and uric acid kidney stones. Serum urate can be normal during an attack, so crystals are the standard for diagnosis.
whyNot: Weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals are calcium pyrophosphate, seen in pseudogout.
Urate crystals are needle shaped but negatively birefringent. Strong positive birefringence does not fit urate.
Flat plates with notched corners are cholesterol crystals, found in chronic effusions such as long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before this attack, his 24-hour urinary uric acid excretion on a regular diet was 410 mg/day (people who overproduce urate typically excrete more than 800 mg/day). Which of the following best explains his hyperuricemia?
options: Increased de novo purine synthesis from HGPRT deficiency
Increased cell turnover releasing nucleic acid purines
Reduced renal urate excretion from thiazide therapy
Excess urate production from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency
approach: Compare urinary uric acid with serum urate. A high serum level with normal urinary output means the kidney is not clearing urate well.
About 90 percent of gout comes from underexcretion.
Thiazides cause volume contraction and compete with urate for tubular secretion, so net reabsorption rises.
questions.why: Uric acid is the end product of purine breakdown: xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. Serum urate rises from overproduction or, far more often, from reduced renal excretion. Thiazide and loop diuretics cause volume contraction and compete with urate at organic anion transporters in the proximal tubule. A normal 24-hour urinary uric acid with a high serum urate shows underexcretion here, and alcohol and purine-rich meat added to the load that night.
whyNot: HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan syndrome) blocks purine salvage, raises de novo synthesis, and causes overproduction with high urinary uric acid, usually in boys with neurologic disease.
High cell turnover, as in tumor lysis or myeloproliferative disease, causes overproduction with high urinary uric acid.
Correct.
Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) raises urate and appears in childhood with hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.

questions.stem: Neutrophils fill the joint within hours after crystals are shed into it. Which of the following events in synovial macrophages most directly starts this inflammation?
options: NLRP3 inflammasome activation releasing IL-1 beta
IgE cross-linking on mast cells releasing histamine
Immune complexes fixing complement in vessel walls
Sensitized CD4 T cells releasing interferon gamma
approach: Urate crystals are a danger signal recognized by innate immunity, with no need for prior sensitization.
Macrophages take up the crystals, which activates the NLRP3 inflammasome and caspase-1.
Caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1 beta to IL-1 beta, which recruits neutrophils and drives the rapid, intense attack.
questions.why: Synovial macrophages take up monosodium urate crystals, which activate the NLRP3 inflammasome. This complex activates caspase-1, which cleaves pro-IL-1 beta into active IL-1 beta. IL-1 beta activates endothelium, triggers more cytokines, and brings in large numbers of neutrophils within hours. Because this is innate immunity, no prior exposure is needed, which explains the sudden onset of attacks.
whyNot: Correct.
IgE-mediated mast cell release is type I hypersensitivity, as in allergy and anaphylaxis.
Immune complex deposition with complement is type III hypersensitivity, as in SLE or serum sickness.
Sensitized CD4 T cells releasing interferon gamma is type IV hypersensitivity, which develops over days.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman seen the same day has an acutely swollen knee. Her joint fluid shows rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence, and a knee radiograph shows linear calcification of the menisci. Which of the following conditions is most strongly associated with her disorder?
options: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
Hemochromatosis
Tumor lysis syndrome
Thiazide diuretic use
approach: Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals with chondrocalcinosis identify calcium pyrophosphate deposition, or pseudogout.
Pseudogout usually affects older adults, most often the knee and wrist.
Its classic metabolic associations are hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and hypomagnesemia. The other choices raise urate and cause gout.
questions.why: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals form in cartilage and cause chondrocalcinosis, the linear calcification of menisci and articular cartilage seen on radiographs. Acute attacks mimic gout but usually strike the knee or wrist of older adults. Hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism are classic associations, as are hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatasia. Gout instead favors the first MTP joint and is linked to hyperuricemia.
whyNot: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome causes urate overproduction and gout.
Correct.
Tumor lysis releases nucleic acids that raise urate and can cause gout and uric acid nephropathy.
Thiazides reduce urate excretion and promote gout. They are not a recognized cause of calcium pyrophosphate deposition.

case: A 54-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 3 months of increasing difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, and lifting her arms to wash her hair. She has also had a rash on her face and hands, abdominal bloating, early satiety, and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss. Physical examination shows a violaceous rash on the upper eyelids with periorbital edema and raised, scaly, violet papules over the knuckles. Strength is 4-/5 in the hip flexors and deltoids and 5/5 distally. Serum creatine kinase is 2,850 U/L (30 to 170). Serum CA-125 is 410 U/mL (under 35), and imaging shows a left adnexal mass. Biopsy confirms high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma. Diagnosis: dermatomyositis associated with ovarian cancer.

questions.stem: A deltoid muscle biopsy shows atrophy of fibers at the edges of the fascicles and inflammation around perimysial vessels. Which of the following immune mechanisms best explains this pattern?
options: Complement attack on intramuscular capillaries
CD8 T cell lysis of fibers that express MHC class I
Antibody blockade of acetylcholine receptors
Granulomas formed by activated macrophages
approach: Atrophy at the edges of fascicles, called perifascicular atrophy, is the signature of dermatomyositis.
In dermatomyositis, antibodies and the membrane attack complex injure endomysial capillaries, which drop out.
Fibers at the fascicle edges are farthest from the remaining blood supply, so they become ischemic and shrink.
questions.why: Dermatomyositis is a complement-driven injury of small vessels. Membrane attack complex is deposited on endomysial capillaries, which are lost. The watershed fibers at the edge of each fascicle become ischemic and atrophic, giving perifascicular atrophy, with CD4 T cells and B cells around perimysial vessels. Polymyositis instead shows CD8 T cells invading fibers within the endomysium. Both cause proximal weakness and a high CK, and both can come with anti-Jo-1 antibodies and interstitial lung disease. Dermatomyositis in adults is linked to cancers such as ovarian, lung, and gastric carcinoma.
whyNot: Correct.
CD8 T cell invasion of fibers that express MHC class I is the mechanism of polymyositis, which lacks perifascicular atrophy.
Antibodies against acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis, with fatigable ptosis and a normal CK.
Granulomas in muscle suggest sarcoidosis. They do not produce perifascicular atrophy.

questions.stem: She develops difficulty starting a swallow, with coughing and nasal regurgitation of liquids. Which of the following histologic features describes the normal muscle tissue responsible for this symptom?
options: Branched fibers with central nuclei and intercalated discs
Fusiform cells with central nuclei and no striations
Striated fibers with central nuclei and dyads
Long striated fibers with many peripheral nuclei
approach: Trouble starting a swallow with nasal regurgitation points to weakness of the pharynx and upper esophagus.
These muscles are skeletal muscle, so inflammatory myositis can weaken them.
Skeletal muscle fibers are long, striated, and multinucleated, with nuclei at the periphery.
questions.why: The pharyngeal constrictors and the upper third of the esophagus are skeletal muscle, the middle third is mixed, and the lower third is smooth muscle. Myositis weakens the striated muscles, so the result is difficulty starting a swallow, coughing, and nasal regurgitation. Skeletal muscle fibers are long, multinucleated cells with peripheral nuclei and triads of T tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum. Cardiac muscle has branched cells with central nuclei and intercalated discs, and smooth muscle has fusiform cells with a central nucleus and no striations.
whyNot: Branched fibers with central nuclei and intercalated discs are cardiac muscle.
Fusiform cells without striations are smooth muscle, found in the lower esophagus. Weakness there slows passage of food through the chest and does not impair starting a swallow.
Central nuclei with dyads describe cardiac muscle, where each T tubule pairs with one sarcoplasmic reticulum cisterna.
Correct.

topics: Histology of skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle

questions.stem: In polymyositis, by contrast, biopsy shows CD8 T cells surrounding and invading non-necrotic muscle fibers. Which of the following types of hypersensitivity best describes the injury in polymyositis?
options: Type II, antibodies against cell surface antigens
Type IV, T cell-mediated cytotoxicity
Type III, immune complex deposition
Type I, IgE-mediated mast cell release
approach: Classify by effector: IgE (type I), antibody against fixed antigen (type II), immune complexes (type III), and T cells (type IV).
In polymyositis, muscle fibers display MHC class I, and CD8 T cells recognize and kill them.
Injury carried out by T cells without antibody is type IV hypersensitivity.
questions.why: Type IV hypersensitivity is injury caused by T cells, either CD4 T cells that release cytokines or CD8 T cells that kill target cells directly. In polymyositis, muscle fibers up-regulate MHC class I, and CD8 T cells with perforin and granzymes invade and destroy them. Other musculoskeletal examples: rheumatic fever polyarthritis and Lambert-Eaton syndrome are type II, and SLE arthritis is type III.
whyNot: Type II reactions use antibodies against fixed cell or matrix antigens, as in rheumatic fever and Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
Correct.
Type III reactions come from circulating immune complexes, as in SLE arthritis.
Type I reactions are immediate IgE-driven responses such as anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: In her intact deltoid fibers, a motor nerve impulse still triggers contraction. Which of the following events directly links T-tubule depolarization to calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in these fibers?
options: Calcium entry through L-type channels triggering RyR2
IP3 binding to receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Dihydropyridine receptor shape change opening RyR1
Calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light chain kinase
approach: Skeletal muscle couples voltage to calcium release mechanically.
The dihydropyridine receptor in the T tubule acts as a voltage sensor and is physically linked to ryanodine receptor 1 in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Calcium then binds troponin C, and SERCA later pumps it back to end the contraction.
questions.why: In skeletal muscle, the action potential spreads down the T tubules and changes the shape of the dihydropyridine receptor, an L-type calcium channel that works mainly as a voltage sensor. It is mechanically coupled to ryanodine receptor 1 on the terminal cisternae, which opens and releases calcium. No calcium entry from outside the cell is required. Calcium binds troponin C, tropomyosin moves aside, and cross-bridges form. SERCA pumps calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum for relaxation.
whyNot: Calcium-induced calcium release through L-type channels and RyR2 is how cardiac muscle couples excitation to contraction.
IP3-mediated release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum contributes to smooth muscle contraction.
Correct.
Calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light chain kinase drives smooth muscle contraction. Skeletal muscle uses troponin C.

dx: Polymyalgia rheumatica with giant cell arteritis
case: A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 6 weeks of aching and stiffness in both shoulders, her neck, and both hips. Morning stiffness lasts about 2 hours, and she needs help getting out of bed. For 2 weeks she has also had a new right-sided headache, scalp tenderness when combing her hair, and jaw pain when chewing. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F). Physical examination shows painful, limited active shoulder abduction, with full strength when pain is controlled. The right temporal artery is tender and thickened with a reduced pulse. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 86 mm/h (0 to 30), C-reactive protein is 5.8 mg/dL (0 to 0.8), and serum creatine kinase is 62 U/L (30 to 170). Diagnosis: polymyalgia rheumatica with giant cell arteritis.

questions.stem: Without prompt treatment, she is at greatest risk for permanent vision loss. Which of the following mechanisms most likely causes this complication?
options: Thrombosis of the central retinal vein
Compression of the optic chiasm by a pituitary mass
Occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries
Acute closure of the anterior chamber angle
approach: Headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and an abnormal temporal artery in a patient with polymyalgia rheumatica indicate giant cell arteritis.
The arteritis involves branches of the external carotid and ophthalmic arteries.
Narrowing of the short posterior ciliary arteries cuts off blood to the optic nerve head, causing ischemic optic neuropathy and sudden vision loss.
questions.why: Polymyalgia rheumatica occurs in adults over 50, more often women, with shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, a high ESR, and a normal CK. About 15 to 20 percent of patients also have giant cell arteritis, a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium arteries. Narrowing of the posterior ciliary arteries, branches of the ophthalmic artery, starves the optic nerve head and causes arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Vision loss is sudden and often permanent.
whyNot: Central retinal vein occlusion causes painless vision loss with widespread retinal hemorrhages and is linked to hypertension and diabetes.
A pituitary mass compresses the chiasm and causes a slowly developing bitemporal hemianopia.
Correct.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye with a fixed, mid-dilated pupil. It is not caused by arteritis.

topics: Polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis
Blood supply of the optic nerve head

questions.stem: A colleague suggests polymyositis as an alternative diagnosis. Which of the following findings in this patient argues most strongly against inflammatory myositis?
options: Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Normal serum creatine kinase
Symmetric proximal girdle involvement
Onset after the age of 50 years
approach: Inflammatory myositis destroys muscle fibers, which releases creatine kinase into the blood.
Polymyalgia rheumatica inflames bursae, tendon sheaths, and joints around the girdles, and spares the muscle fibers.
A normal CK with full strength points away from myositis.
questions.why: Polymyositis and dermatomyositis cause true proximal weakness from myofiber necrosis, so CK is high, often many times normal, and biopsy shows inflammatory infiltrates. In polymyalgia rheumatica, the apparent weakness comes from pain, and CK and muscle biopsy are normal. Steroid myopathy is another cause of proximal weakness with a normal CK, but it is painless and follows corticosteroid use.
whyNot: ESR can be high in both conditions, so it does not separate them.
Correct.
Both disorders affect the shoulder and hip girdles on both sides.
Polymyalgia rheumatica requires age over 50, but myositis also occurs at this age.

topics: Polymyalgia rheumatica compared with inflammatory myositis

questions.stem: Ultrasound of her shoulder shows inflammation of the subacromial bursa around the tendon that passes under the acromion and starts abduction of the arm. Which of the following nerves innervates the muscle of this tendon?
options: Axillary nerve
Upper subscapular nerve
Long thoracic nerve
Suprascapular nerve
approach: The tendon under the acromion that starts abduction belongs to supraspinatus.
Supraspinatus starts abduction for about the first 15 degrees, and deltoid takes over after that.
Supraspinatus and infraspinatus are both supplied by the suprascapular nerve.
questions.why: Supraspinatus runs from the supraspinous fossa under the acromion to the greater tubercle. It starts abduction and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5 to C6), as is infraspinatus, a lateral rotator. Teres minor, also a lateral rotator, is supplied by the axillary nerve, and subscapularis, a medial rotator, by the subscapular nerves. Its course under the acromion makes supraspinatus the rotator cuff tendon most often injured, and the subacromial bursa next to it is often inflamed in polymyalgia rheumatica.
whyNot: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid, which abducts the arm after the first 15 degrees, and teres minor.
The subscapular nerves supply subscapularis, a medial rotator, and teres major.
The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior. Injury causes a winged scapula.
Correct.

questions.stem: She is treated with high-dose prednisone. Five months later her girdle pain has resolved, but she has painless, progressive difficulty rising from a chair. Serum creatine kinase is 48 U/L (30 to 170). A muscle biopsy would most likely show which of the following?
options: Type II fiber atrophy without inflammation
Grouped atrophy with fiber type grouping
Ragged red fibers on Gomori trichrome stain
Endomysial lymphocytes with necrotic fibers
approach: Painless proximal weakness with a normal CK after months of high-dose corticosteroids suggests steroid myopathy.
Corticosteroids increase protein breakdown and reduce protein synthesis, mostly in fast glycolytic fibers.
The biopsy shows selective type II fiber atrophy with no necrosis or inflammation, the same pattern seen with disuse.
questions.why: Long-term glucocorticoids cause catabolic muscle wasting that falls mostly on type II (fast, glycolytic) fibers. The result is painless proximal weakness, especially of the hip flexors, with a normal CK because fibers shrink without dying. Biopsy shows type II fiber atrophy without inflammation. Neurogenic disease instead shows grouped atrophy and fiber type grouping, and inflammatory myopathy shows necrosis and infiltrates with a high CK.
whyNot: Correct.
Grouped atrophy and fiber type grouping mean denervation and reinnervation, as in spinal muscular atrophy, usually with fasciculations.
Ragged red fibers reflect abnormal mitochondria in mitochondrial myopathies such as MERRF.
Endomysial lymphocytes with necrotic fibers indicate inflammatory myositis, which would raise CK.

dx: Reactive arthritis after Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis
case: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of 5 days of pain and swelling in his right knee and left ankle. Three weeks ago he had dysuria and a urethral discharge, and a nucleic acid amplification test of urine was positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. He also reports red, irritated eyes and pain in both heels. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F). Physical examination shows bilateral conjunctival injection, a warm knee effusion, a swollen left ankle, and tenderness at the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia insertions. Knee aspiration yields fluid with 16,000 leukocytes/mm3, mostly neutrophils, and no crystals. Gram stain and culture are negative. HLA-B27 testing is positive. Diagnosis: reactive arthritis after Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the arthritis in this patient?
options: Replication of viable bacteria within the synovium
Immune reaction after a distant infection
Autoantibodies against citrullinated synovial proteins
Deposition of crystals within the joint cavity
approach: Arthritis that starts weeks after urethritis, with conjunctivitis and enthesitis, fits reactive arthritis.
The synovial culture is negative and no crystals are present, so the joint is neither infected nor affected by crystal disease.
In HLA-B27 positive hosts, the immune response to bacterial antigens from a distant site drives a sterile arthritis.
questions.why: Reactive arthritis is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that follows infection elsewhere, usually Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis or enteric infection with Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, or Campylobacter. Bacterial antigens, and sometimes nonviable bacterial fragments, reach the joint, and HLA-B27 carriers mount a persistent immune response. Typical features are asymmetric arthritis of the lower limbs, conjunctivitis, urethritis, enthesitis, dactylitis, and keratoderma blennorrhagicum on the soles.
whyNot: Live bacteria in the joint is septic arthritis, which would give a positive Gram stain or culture. In sexually active young adults, Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a common cause.
Correct.
Antibodies to citrullinated peptides drive rheumatoid arthritis, a symmetric small joint arthritis linked to HLA-DR4.
Crystal arthritis (gout or pseudogout) is excluded because no crystals are present.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old kindergarten teacher develops symmetric pain and swelling of the MCP joints, PIP joints, and wrists. Two weeks earlier, several children in her class had bright red cheeks followed by a lacy rash on the arms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her arthritis?
options: Disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae
HLA-B27 associated reactive arthritis
Parvovirus B19 infection
Recent rubella vaccination
approach: Bright red cheeks followed by a lacy rash in children is erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease.
In adults, especially women, parvovirus B19 often causes a symmetric small joint arthritis.
Symmetric hand arthritis after exposure to children with fifth disease points to parvovirus.
questions.why: Parvovirus B19 causes fifth disease in children. Adults, especially women, often develop a symmetric arthritis of the hands, wrists, and knees that can mimic rheumatoid arthritis and usually resolves within weeks. Rubella infection, and less often rubella vaccination, causes a similar short-lived arthralgia in adult women. Reactive arthritis follows enteric or chlamydial infection in HLA-B27 carriers and is usually asymmetric and in the lower limbs.
whyNot: Disseminated gonococcal infection causes tenosynovitis, pustular skin lesions, and migratory arthralgia or purulent monoarthritis in sexually active young adults.
Reactive arthritis is usually asymmetric and affects large lower-limb joints after genitourinary or enteric infection.
Correct.
Rubella vaccination can cause brief arthralgia in adult women, but no vaccine is mentioned and her exposure fits fifth disease.

questions.stem: His 52-year-old father has scaly plaques on the elbows, pitted fingernails, and swelling of several distal interphalangeal joints. A radiograph of the father's hands would most likely show which of the following?
options: Pencil-in-cup erosions at the DIP joints
Periarticular osteopenia with erosions at the MCP joints
Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges
Osteophytes with joint space narrowing at the DIP joints
approach: Skin plaques, nail pitting, and DIP arthritis identify psoriatic arthritis.
Psoriatic arthritis combines erosion with new bone formation, and severe erosion at the DIP joint gives a pencil-in-cup shape.
Rheumatoid arthritis spares the DIP joints and shows periarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions at the MCP and PIP joints.
questions.why: Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy. It typically involves the DIP joints, causes dactylitis (sausage digits) and nail pitting, and can involve the spine, a pattern linked to HLA-B27. Radiographs show erosions with new bone formation nearby, and advanced disease produces pencil-in-cup deformities. Rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetric MCP and PIP arthritis that spares the DIP joints, with periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions, and positive rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP.
whyNot: Correct.
Periarticular osteopenia with MCP erosions is the pattern of rheumatoid arthritis, which spares the DIP joints.
Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges are typical of chronic tophaceous gout.
Osteophytes at the DIP joints (Heberden nodes) mark osteoarthritis, which does not cause nail pitting or skin plaques.

topics: Psoriatic arthritis compared with rheumatoid arthritis

questions.stem: His heel pain arises at the attachment of the plantar aponeurosis to the calcaneus. Long-term failure of this support, together with the spring ligament and tibialis posterior, would most likely produce which of the following deformities?
options: Pes cavus from an exaggerated longitudinal arch
Hallux valgus from lateral deviation of the great toe
Talipes equinovarus with plantarflexion and inversion
Pes planus from medial longitudinal arch collapse
approach: The plantar aponeurosis acts like a tie-beam between the calcaneus and the toes, holding up the longitudinal arches.
The medial longitudinal arch is also held by the spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament under the head of the talus and by the tibialis posterior tendon.
When these supports fail, the medial arch collapses and the foot becomes flat.
questions.why: The foot has medial and lateral longitudinal arches and a transverse arch. The medial longitudinal arch is the highest and depends on the plantar aponeurosis, the spring ligament under the head of the talus, and the tibialis posterior tendon. When these weaken, the arch collapses and the foot becomes flat (pes planus), often with the heel turned outward. Pes cavus is the opposite, an abnormally high arch.
whyNot: Pes cavus is an abnormally high arch, often from neuromuscular disease such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Loss of arch support does the opposite.
Hallux valgus is lateral deviation of the great toe at the first MTP joint, linked to narrow footwear. It does not come from loss of arch support.
Talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) is a congenital deformity present at birth.
Correct.
